title: ClickFix finger Lure to CastleLoader and a Hollowed node.exe Agent
subtitle: A finger.exe paste runs a five-stage loader. The C2 picks which runs get tasks. The ones that do get NetSupport and a Rust agent running inside a second node.exe.

meta.v: How the agent learned its C2

nodes.label: ClickFix finger paste
nodes.desc: The paste runs finger.exe against the lure server and executes the lines that come back as a batch script.

nodes.label: IronPython stager
nodes.sub: Batch pulls IronPython, runs packed Python
nodes.desc: The batch pulls IronPython 3.4.2 from GitHub, kills and restarts explorer.exe, and runs a zlib + base64 Python one-liner with ipyw32 -c. The Python downloads timer3 with certificate checks off and execs it.

nodes.label: timer3 shellcode
nodes.sub: XOR'd shellcode run from an executable heap
nodes.desc: timer3 hides its Base64 behind sprinkled Cyrillic letters, XORs out a 6 KB shellcode with a 23-byte key and runs it from an executable heap. The shellcode finds its APIs by hash, fetches /v3 and RC4-decrypts it with the file's own first 64 bytes.

nodes.label: CastleLoader core
nodes.sub: Embedded PE mapped into its own process
nodes.desc: Stage 2 takes control through a ReplaceTextW dialog hook and maps an embedded PE in memory: the CastleLoader core. It crashes itself on a CIS-language system unless a marker file exists, and on VMware when the tasking turns that check on.
nodes.notes: Family name is Moderate confidence: ANY.RUN, VirusTotal and Hybrid Analysis tag it CastleLoader and eleven details match published analysis.

nodes.label: Server-side tasking
nodes.sub: ChaCha20 get_tasks. 2 of 5 runs got tasks
nodes.desc: The core fetches settings with a 31-character token as the User-Agent, then talks ChaCha20 over base64. The key and nonce are constants in the code, so every captured check-in decodes. Two runs were handed three tasks. Three got nothing; the empty reply I decoded reads tasks: {}.
nodes.notes: High confidence the server decided. Why it picked those two runs is unknown.

nodes.label: NetSupport Manager
nodes.sub: Genuine client, silent, gateways on port 725
nodes.desc: One task pulls an RC4-encrypted ZIP of genuine NetSupport Manager files, set up silent with two gateways. client32.exe started from a scheduled task at T+6 min.

nodes.label: Hollowed node.exe
nodes.sub: index.js decrypts two blobs. Agent runs in a 2nd node.exe
nodes.desc: The other task drops node.exe, an obfuscated index.js and two GUID-named .tmp files in C:\ProgramData\NodeView. index.js is only a launcher: it decrypts both files with AES-256-GCM and starts blob 1, which hollows a second node.exe with blob 2. Blob 2 is onedriveupdater.exe, a 19.5 MB Rust agent that talks WebSocket to its own C2.
nodes.notes: Open: how the agent learned homelygrill[.]com. The name is not in the file in any encoding I tried, and the Steam dead-drop resolver in the code never fired.

nodes.label: Scheduled tasks
nodes.desc: The agent persists with a logon task, \WebViewNode, and \RuntimeUtil every two hours, a reinstaller that re-downloads from liokida[.]com.

nodes.label: Keylogging and theft
nodes.desc: The server pushes keyboard-monitor rules for 35 process names: browsers, wallets, password managers. The agent also offers a hidden-desktop remote viewer, webcam, a remote shell, and browser, wallet and Telegram theft uploaded as data.zip.
nodes.notes: The theft features are read from the code. The sandbox flagged credential and wallet access (wallet access at T+16 min).

nodes.label: Phone Link pairing?
nodes.desc: The --plnag copy of the agent shows a fake Windows Phone Link first-run window whose buttons open the real app. It is probably meant to get a phone paired.
nodes.notes: Not confirmed. A run where a phone gets paired, or the code that uses a paired phone, would settle it.
